subject: Millennium Bridge London
title: What If Walking Made a Bridge Sway? London's Did, and People Made It Worse

scenes.text: What if a bridge swayed under your feet? London's did on opening day. The crowd made it worse.
June 10th, 2000. Around 80,000 people crossed the new Millennium Bridge, up to 2,000 at a time.
It began to sway side to side, about once a second. Right at the rhythm of a human walking.
To keep their balance, people widened their stance and fell into step with the sway. Thousands of feet pushing in unison.
Scientists later found the tipping point: about 160 people walking together is enough to lock a crowd into step.
The bridge closed after two days. Five million pounds of dampers later, it reopened in 2002. The wobble is gone. The nickname never left.

description:
What if walking made a bridge sway? On 10 June 2000 London's Millennium Bridge began swinging side to side under its opening-day crowd of about 80,000.
Its sway frequency, about one cycle a second, matched a walking pace; people unconsciously fell into step to steady themselves, which fed the motion. Cornell's Steven Strogatz (Nature, 2005) calculated that about 160 walkers can trigger it. The bridge closed after two days and reopened in 2002 after a 5 million pound damper retrofit.

first_comment: Londoners still call it the Wobbly Bridge. The original design cost about 32 million dollars; the fix cost nearly 9 million more. Which engineering what-if should we run through next?
